lessons.title: Division Expressions with Fractions and Whole Numbers
lessons.objective: I can divide a whole number by a unit fraction and divide a fraction by a whole number by writing the whole number over 1 and using Keep, Change, Flip.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain each step of Keep, Change, Flip using the words reciprocal, divisor, and quotient.

concept.heading: What does it mean to divide by a fraction?
concept.intro: Dividing by a fraction asks one question: how many of that small piece fit inside the whole amount? For 3 ÷ 1/4, we ask how many 1/4-foot pieces fit into 3 feet.
concept.keyIdea: Dividing Whole Numbers & Fractions. 1. Put a 1 under the whole number: 3 ÷ 1/4 = 3/1 ÷ 1/4. 2. Keep, Change, Flip: 3/1 ÷ 1/4 = 3/1 × 4/1. 3. Multiply across: 3/1 × 4/1 = 12/1 = 12

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I want to cut a 3-foot strip of tape into 1/4-foot pieces, so I write 3 ÷ 1/4.
The 3 is a whole number, so I put a 1 under it. Now both numbers are fractions: 3/1 ÷ 1/4.
Keep, Change, Flip. I keep 3/1, I change ÷ to ×, and I flip 1/4 to 4/1. That gives 3/1 × 4/1.
I multiply across: 3 × 4 = 12 on top and 1 × 1 = 1 on the bottom, so 3 ÷ 1/4 = 3/1 × 4/1 = 12 pieces.
One more move to know: mixed number → improper fraction: multiply the bottom by the whole number, add the top, keep the same bottom. 3 1/2 → (2 × 3) + 1 = 7 → 7/2.
linesEs: Quiero cortar una tira de cinta de 3 pies en piezas de 1/4 de pie, así que escribo 3 ÷ 1/4.
El 3 es un número entero, así que le pongo un 1 debajo. Ahora los dos números son fracciones: 3/1 ÷ 1/4.
Conserva, Cambia, Voltea. Conservo 3/1, cambio ÷ por × y volteo 1/4 a 4/1. Eso da 3/1 × 4/1.
Multiplico en línea: 3 × 4 = 12 arriba y 1 × 1 = 1 abajo, así que 3 ÷ 1/4 = 3/1 × 4/1 = 12 piezas.
Un movimiento más que debes saber: número mixto → fracción impropia: multiplica el denominador por el entero, suma el numerador y conserva el mismo denominador. 3 1/2 → (2 × 3) + 1 = 7 → 7/2.

together.title: Let's do one together — the same problem the bar model showed
lines: Let's try 2 ÷ 1/3. The bar model counted 6 thirds inside 2 wholes — now we get there with the steps.
Step 1: put a 1 under the whole number. 2 becomes 2/1, so we have 2/1 ÷ 1/3.
Step 2: Keep, Change, Flip. Keep 2/1, change ÷ to ×, flip 1/3 to 3/1. That gives 2/1 × 3/1.
Step 3: multiply across. 2 × 3 = 6 on top and 1 × 1 = 1 on the bottom, so 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6 — exactly what we counted on the bars.
linesEs: Probemos 2 ÷ 1/3. El modelo de barras contó 6 tercios dentro de 2 enteros; ahora llegamos ahí con los pasos.
Paso 1: pon un 1 debajo del número entero. El 2 se vuelve 2/1, así que tenemos 2/1 ÷ 1/3.
Paso 2: Conserva, Cambia, Voltea. Conserva 2/1, cambia ÷ por ×, voltea 1/3 a 3/1. Eso da 2/1 × 3/1.
Paso 3: multiplica en línea. 2 × 3 = 6 arriba y 1 × 1 = 1 abajo, así que 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6, exactamente lo que contamos en las barras.
together.titleEs: Hagamos uno juntos — el mismo problema que mostró el modelo de barras

vocabulary.definition: Finding how many groups of one fraction fit inside another amount.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction turned upside down.
vocabulary.example: The reciprocal of 1/4 is 4/1 = 4. A whole number like 3 is 3/1, so its reciprocal is 1/3.

vocabulary.definition: The answer when you divide.
vocabulary.example: In 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12, the quotient is 12 — there are 12 quarter-size pieces in 3

vocabulary.definition: The total number being divided into equal groups (the number inside the division bracket).
vocabulary.example: In 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12, the dividend is 3 — it is the total being split

vocabulary.definition: The number of equal groups you are dividing into (the number outside the division bracket).

lessons.title: Division Expressions with Fractions and Mixed Numbers
lessons.objective: I can divide a fraction by a fraction and divide with mixed numbers by multiplying by the reciprocal.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain the steps using the words reciprocal, improper fraction, mixed number, and simplify.

concept.heading: How do I divide one fraction by another fraction?
concept.intro: When you divide a fraction by a fraction, you keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, and flip the second fraction (the divisor) to its reciprocal. Then multiply and simplify.
concept.keyIdea: Dividing Fractions Algorithm (Keep, Change, Flip). Formula: a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c. 1. Keep the first fraction unchanged. 2. Change the division symbol (÷) to multiplication (×). 3. Flip the second fraction to its reciprocal (d/c), then multiply across and simplify

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Agent Rivera has 3/4 pound and each portion is 1/8 pound. I want 3/4 ÷ 1/8.
Keep 3/4. Change ÷ to ×. Flip the divisor 1/8 to its reciprocal 8/1.
Simplify: 24/4 = 6. So 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6. She can make 6 portions.
One more move to know: mixed number → improper fraction: multiply the bottom by the whole number, add the top, keep the same bottom. 3 1/2 → (2 × 3) + 1 = 7 → 7/2.
linesEs: El agente Rivera tiene 3/4 de libra y cada porción es de 1/8 de libra. Quiero 3/4 ÷ 1/8.
Mantengo 3/4. Cambio ÷ por ×. Invierto el divisor 1/8 para obtener su recíproco 8/1.
Un movimiento más que debes saber: número mixto → fracción impropia: multiplica el denominador por el entero, suma el numerador y conserva el mismo denominador. 3 1/2 → (2 × 3) + 1 = 7 → 7/2.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's try 1/2 ÷ 1/4. Keep 1/2, change to ×, flip 1/4 to 4/1.
linesEs: Probemos 1/2 ÷ 1/4. Mantén 1/2, cambia a ×, invierte 1/4 a 4/1.

support.explanation: 3 ÷ 1/4 asks how many 1/4-size pieces fit into 3. To find that, put a 1 under the 3 and use Keep, Change, Flip: 3/1 × 4/1 = 12.
feedback: That's finding a part of the whole. Division by a fraction asks 'how many of this size fit inside.'
That's multiplication (3 × 1/4). Division asks 'how many' pieces, not 'groups of' pieces.
Subtraction is not division. Division by a fraction asks 'how many pieces fit.'
hints: Re-read the expression: 3 is the total amount and 1/4 is the size of one piece. What question could that setup be asking?
Dividing by a fraction asks a counting question about pieces, not 'a part of.' Predict: should the result be bigger or smaller than 3?
Picture a 3-foot tape cut into 1/4-foot pieces, then set it up: put a 1 under the 3 and flip the 1/4.

support.prompt: Which expression means 'how many 1/3-size pieces are in 2'?
support.explanation: Finding how many 1/3-size pieces fit into 2 is written 2 ÷ 1/3. Put a 1 under the 2, then Keep, Change, Flip: 2/1 × 3/1 = 6.
feedback: You flipped the order. The whole (2) goes first; the piece size (1/3) is the divisor.
That multiplies instead of divides. To find how many pieces fit, we divide by the piece size.
Addition combines amounts. To find how many pieces fit, we divide.
hints: Find the two jobs: which number is the total being split, and which is the size of each piece?
Division setups read total ÷ piece size. The total always sits in front of the ÷ sign.
Here the total is 2 and each piece is 1/3. Build the expression with the total first, then check it against each choice.

support.prompt: A rope is 4 feet long. How many 1/2-foot pieces can be cut from it?
support.explanation: Write 4 ÷ 1/2. Put a 1 under the 4, then Keep, Change, Flip: 4/1 × 2/1 = 8 pieces.
feedback: You did not flip the divisor. Put a 1 under the 4, flip 1/2 to 2/1, then multiply.
You divided 4 by 2. Dividing by 1/2 means flipping it: 4/1 × 2/1 = 8.
Dividing by 1/2 makes the answer bigger. Flipping 1/2 gives 2/1, a factor larger than 1.
hints: Note the numbers: the rope is 4 feet long, and every piece is 1/2 foot — smaller than a whole foot.
Start small: figure out how many 1/2-foot pieces fit into just 1 foot of rope.
Put a 1 under the 4 to get 4/1, then Keep, Change, Flip: 4/1 × 2/1.

support.prompt: A half-pan of brownies is shared equally among 4 people. How much of the whole pan does each get?
support.explanation: This is 1/2 ÷ 4. The whole number is second this time, so put a 1 under the 4, then Keep, Change, Flip: 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8 of the whole pan.
feedback: That gives the whole half to one person instead of sharing it.
That divides 4 by 1/2 — the opposite question.
That flips the problem into a multiplication of the wrong pair.
hints: Draw half a pan, then split that half into 4 equal parts.
How many of those parts fit in the WHOLE pan?
The whole number is second here. Put a 1 under the 4 to get 4/1, then flip it to 1/4 and multiply.

steps: Problem: How many 1/3-foot pieces fit into 4 feet of tape? Find 4 ÷ 1/3.
Student writes: Dividing makes the answer smaller, so 4 ÷ 1/3 = 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.3 pieces.
support.explanation: Put a 1 under the whole number, then Keep, Change, Flip: 4/1 × 3/1 = 12 pieces. Flipping the divisor 1/3 gives 3/1, so the answer grows.
hints: How many 1/3-foot pieces fit inside just ONE foot?
If the pieces are smaller than a whole foot, will MORE or FEWER than 4 fit into 4 feet?

support.explanation: To find the reciprocal, flip the fraction. The reciprocal of 3/5 is 5/3.
feedback: That flips only the 3. A reciprocal flips the WHOLE fraction, so both the 3 and the 5 change places.
That is the original fraction, unflipped. A reciprocal swaps the top and bottom numbers, so 3/5 becomes 5/3.
The bottom number was used for both spots. Keep both numbers — just trade their places: the 3 moves down, the 5 moves up.
hints: Re-read 'reciprocal' — it's about the two numbers of the fraction trading places.
Swap the numerator (top number) with the denominator (bottom number). Nothing else changes.
In 3/5, the 3 is on top and the 5 is on the bottom. Trade their spots and match the result to a choice.

feedback: That's multiplication or another operation. Division asks 'how many of this size fit in the whole.'

1/4 flips to 4/1, so multiply 1/2 × 4/1 across the tops and bottoms, then simplify your fraction.

support.prompt: What is the first step in evaluating 2 1/2 ÷ 1/4?
choices: Divide 2 by 1/4 and ignore the half
support.explanation: A mixed number cannot be flipped or multiplied as it stands, so rewrite it first: 2 1/2 = 5/2. Then Keep, Change, Flip gives 5/2 × 4/1 = 10.
feedback: A mixed number has no single numerator and denominator to flip.
Dropping the half changes the problem into a different one.
Division is not solved by adding the parts.
hints: Which number in this problem is a mixed number?
How many halves are in 2 1/2?
Rewrite it as one fraction before Keep, Change, Flip.

support.explanation: The student tried to divide the tops and bottoms straight across instead of using Keep, Change, Flip. Keep 1/2, change ÷ to ×, and flip the divisor 1/4 to 4/1: 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2. (Even though the answer happens to be 2 here, dividing straight across is not a reliable rule — it breaks for problems like 2/3 ÷ 1/2.)
hints: You cannot divide fractions by dividing the numerators and denominators straight across.
Use Keep, Change, Flip: keep 1/2, change ÷ to ×, and flip the divisor 1/4 to its reciprocal 4/1.

core.prompt: A shelf is 5 feet long. Books are each 1/4 foot wide. How many books fit on the shelf? Which expression represents this?
core.explanation: The expression is 5 ÷ 1/4. Put a 1 under the 5, then Keep, Change, Flip: 5/1 × 4/1 = 20 books.
feedback: You flipped the division. The shelf length (5) is the dividend; the book width (1/4) is the divisor.
That multiplies instead of dividing. To count pieces that fit, divide the whole by the piece size.
Addition combines lengths. To find how many books fit, divide the shelf length by one book's width.
hints: Spot the roles: 5 feet is the whole shelf, and 1/4 foot is the width of one book.
Counting how many books fit means total ÷ piece size — and the count should be bigger than 5, since books are thin.
Set it up as 5 ÷ 1/4, put a 1 under the 5, and flip the divisor to test which choice matches.

core.prompt: A 5/6-mile stretch of the evidence trail is split equally among 3 search teams. How much of a mile does each team walk?
core.explanation: Write 5/6 ÷ 3 as 5/6 ÷ 3/1. Keep, Change, Flip: 5/6 × 1/3 = 5/18 mile for each team. Three teams walking 5/18 mile each covers 15/18 = 5/6 mile, so the answer checks out.
feedback: That splits only ONE sixth among the teams. There are five sixths to share.
That multiplies by 3. Dividing by 3 means writing it as 3/1 and flipping it to 1/3.
That sends every team the whole 5/6 mile instead of splitting it three ways.
hints: Sharing an amount among teams is division: 5/6 ÷ 3.
Write the 3 as 3/1 so both numbers are fractions.
Keep 5/6, change ÷ to ×, flip 3/1 to 1/3, and multiply across.

steps: Problem: How many 1/5-cup scoops fill a 6-cup container? Find 6 ÷ 1/5.
Student writes: I will flip the first number instead of the divisor: 6 ÷ 1/5 = 1/6 × 5 = 5/6 scoop.
core.explanation: Keep, Change, Flip flips the DIVISOR (1/5), not the dividend. Put a 1 under the 6 and flip 1/5 to 5/1: 6/1 × 5/1 = 30 scoops.
hints: Which number do you flip when you divide — the dividend (6) or the divisor (1/5)?

core.prompt: A recipe needs 2/3 cup of sugar. You only have a 1/6-cup scoop. How many scoops do you need?
feedback: Only 2 scoops of 1/6 cup makes 2/6 = 1/3 cup — not enough sugar. Use Keep, Change, Flip on 2/3 ÷ 1/6 and simplify what you get.
Multiplying doesn't answer 'how many fit.' Divide the whole by the piece size.
The dividend (whole) goes first. The divisor (piece size) is second.
hints: The recipe total is 2/3 cup; one scoop holds 1/6 cup — you're counting scoops, not multiplying.
Rewrite 2/3 in sixths so both amounts use the same size pieces.
Multiply top and bottom of 2/3 by 2 to get sixths, then count how many 1/6-scoops that makes.

core.explanation: The student changed ÷ to × but forgot to flip the divisor. Keep 2/3, change ÷ to ×, and flip the divisor 1/2 to its reciprocal 2/1: 2/3 × 2/1 = 4/3 = 1 1/3. The correct quotient is 4/3 (1 1/3), not 1/3.
hints: After you change ÷ to ×, you must also flip the second fraction (the divisor).
The divisor 1/2 should become its reciprocal 2/1 before you multiply: 2/3 × 2/1 = 4/3.

stretch.prompt: Dividing 6 by 1/2 gives 12, but dividing 6 by 2 gives 3. How can dividing by a smaller number (1/2) give a bigger answer than dividing by a larger number (2)? Explain using a real-world example.
stretch.frame: When I divide 6 by 2, I am ___. When I divide 6 by 1/2, I am ___. The answer is bigger because ___.
stretch.explanation: The two expressions ask different questions, and the flip shows why. 6 ÷ 2 is 6/1 × 1/2 = 3, because flipping 2/1 gives a factor smaller than 1. 6 ÷ 1/2 is 6/1 × 2/1 = 12, because flipping 1/2 gives a factor larger than 1. Dividing by a number less than 1 always makes the quotient grow.
hints: Re-read both: 6 ÷ 2 splits 6 into 2 equal groups, but 6 ÷ 1/2 counts how many half-size pieces fit into 6.
Pick a real object — 6 sandwiches shared between 2 people versus 6 sandwiches cut into halves — and describe both.
Start your answer with the sharing story (6 split into 2 groups), then explain what cutting into halves does to the count.

stretch.explanation: The student forgot to flip. 2/5 × 4/3 (flip the divisor 3/4 to get 4/3). Then 2/5 × 4/3 = 8/15.
hints: In 'Keep, Change, Flip' — which fraction gets flipped?

stretch.prompt: Is 3/4 ÷ 1/2 the same as 1/2 ÷ 3/4? Solve both and explain why or why not. What does this tell you about the order in division?
stretch.frame: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = ___ and 1/2 ÷ 3/4 = ___. These are ___ because ___. This shows that division is ___.
stretch.explanation: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 becomes 3/4 × 2/1 = 6/4 = 1 1/2, while 1/2 ÷ 3/4 becomes 1/2 × 4/3 = 4/6 = 2/3, so the two expressions are not equal. Swapping the dividend and the divisor flips the quotient to its reciprocal, which shows that division is not commutative — order matters.
hints: Don't assume the two divisions match — solve each one on its own first.
Use Keep, Change, Flip on both: flip the second fraction each time, then compare the two quotients.
First one: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 → 3/4 × 2/1. Work it out, then set up 1/2 ÷ 3/4 the same way and compare.
